doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

chapter: Black Radio and the new waves
title: The neo-soul wave of the late 1990s
summary: He arrived in New York in 1997, worked with Bilal at Electric Lady, watched D'Angelo make Voodoo and gave Common piano lessons.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah, so I think that there’s been a lot of movement towards infusing jazz and funk into rap and R&B. And it’s not necessarily new, like there’s always been people like © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

D’Angelo and Erykah Badu, but with people like Flying Lotus and Kendrick Lamar obviously and Chance the Rapper who are doing that a lot. And it’s becoming really big. What do you think is the cause of that at this time now in history, being such a big movement that’s happening right now?

Well I think there was two waves of it. I think there was one wave in the early or late 90s, the neo-soul movement. I was in New York when that happened. I didn’t realize it at the time but it was happening. I got to New York in ’97. I met Bilal in ’97. We started working with his album. And we were working on his album at Electric Lady Studios, Jimi Hendrix’s studio. And Erykah was on the — we were on the top floor, Erykah was on the middle floor and D’Angelo was on the bottom floor. So I literally watched D’Angelo make “Voodoo” a lot. I didn’t even know. I was there for that. I was there for comedies like “Water for Chocolate” because Bilal was singing background in that. I didn’t even know Common. In ’99 I didn’t even know who he was. I wasn’t into hard core hip-hop. I came from Texas. I knew Scarface. You know? I knew Ghetto Boys. So I was teaching Common piano lessons. I used to go to his house and give him piano lessons. He lived around the corner. Me, Bilal, Erykah and Common live within four blocks of each other in Brooklyn. So Erykah used to come over my crib and play me stuff, ideas, and, “what do you think about this song, ‘Orange Moon.’” I’m trying to think. Because I was the jazz guy. I was Bilal’s friend who played jazz. And they all was like, “what do you think about this jazz.” And Common was like, “I want to learn jazz.” You know. So I’d give him piano lessons. So that was all a regular thing for me. And I think it was just like a movement. The neo-soul movement happened and live musicians came back and poetry started popping then in ’97.

Spoken word. And spoken word goes right with jazz and that whole thing. There was all that combined. That scene actually happened a block from my house where I used to live a few years ago, in Brooklyn, at the spot called Brooklyn Moon actually. That’s where Saul Williams did his first poem and that’s where Erykah used to go.
